title: DeepSeek develops AI chips, challenging Nvidia and Huawei
text:
DeepSeek develops AI chips, challenging Nvidia and Huawei
JAKARTA - Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) startup DeepSeek is developing its own AI chips to reduce its reliance on products from Nvidia and Huawei, which have so far been used in the development of the company's AI models.
According to Reuters , citing three sources familiar with the plans, DeepSeek's chips are being designed specifically for inference, the stage where trained AI models generate responses for users.
Unlike chips used for model training, inference chips generally consume less power and are designed to meet the growing demand for AI computing.
The move marks a major strategic shift for DeepSeek, which has so far been known for focusing on AI model development rather than the semiconductor business.
If successful, the company would join a number of global AI developers that have begun designing their own chips to gain greater control over computing infrastructure while reducing dependence on Nvidia.
The news briefly weighed on Nvidia shares, which fell around 1.6% in US pre-market trading.
"Nvidia's position in China is effectively at zero and will remain that way. DeepSeek has almost no chance of selling chips outside China unless it gains access to advanced manufacturing technology," said analyst Richard Windsor of Radio Free Mobile, adding that the development would not affect the chipmaker.
DeepSeek attracted global attention in early 2025 after launching a low-cost, high-performance AI model that disrupted the global technology industry.
The Hangzhou-based company has so far been better known for focusing on AI model innovation rather than commercialising the technology it develops.
Amid US restrictions on AI chip exports to China, Huawei has expanded its domestic market share and now controls around half of China's AI chip market, which is valued at approximately US$50 billion.
However, that dominance is increasingly being challenged as several local technology companies, including Alibaba and Baidu, develop their own AI chips.
According to Reuters sources, DeepSeek's chip development project remains at an early stage. Over the past year, the company has been communicating with chip design firms, foundries and memory suppliers to support the development of the semiconductors.
DeepSeek has also increased recruitment of chip design engineers in recent months. The hiring process has been conducted discreetly, without publicly posting job openings on general recruitment platforms.
Despite becoming one of the symbols of China's AI resurgence, DeepSeek has maintained a low profile and has not responded to Reuters' request for confirmation regarding the project.
Globally, DeepSeek's move follows a broader trend among major AI companies developing their own chips. OpenAI introduced its first inference chip, called Jalapeno, last month in collaboration with Broadcom, while Anthropic is also reportedly considering developing its own AI chips.
For DeepSeek, chip development carries greater strategic importance because US export restrictions have prevented Chinese companies from accessing Nvidia's most advanced AI chips.
The Chinese government has also continued to encourage domestic technology companies to build their own semiconductor supply chains.
DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng acknowledged in a 2024 interview that chip export restrictions posed a challenge for the company.
Previously, DeepSeek used a combination of Nvidia and Huawei chips. The base model supporting DeepSeek R1 was trained using Nvidia's H800 chips, a product specifically designed for the Chinese market before the US government banned its export in late 2023.
In recent months, the company has increasingly relied on Huawei's ecosystem. In April, DeepSeek launched its V4 model, which had been optimised for Huawei Ascend chips, while Huawei revealed that training for the V4-Flash model also used Ascend processors.
The launch also drove a surge in demand for Huawei's Ascend 950 chips among Chinese technology companies.
If successfully developed, DeepSeek's inference chips would target the fastest-growing segment of the AI industry.
As the use of AI applications expands, computing demand is shifting from model training towards inference processes that require more efficient and energy-saving chips.
However, developing AI chips is not an easy task. The semiconductor industry requires significant investment and years of development to produce competitive products.
Another challenge comes from US restrictions limiting Chinese companies' access to the most advanced chip manufacturing facilities and high-bandwidth memory (HBM), a key component in modern AI chips.
At the same time, DeepSeek has begun opening itself to external funding. Reuters previously reported that the company was preparing its first funding round worth US$7 billion, with a valuation of between US$52 billion and US$59 billion, ending a years-long strategy of rejecting outside investment. (DH/LM)
